children: The F-35C completed its first launch-and-recovery tests aboard a Gerald R. Ford-class aircraft carrier, advancing efforts to integrate the stealth fighter with the U.S. Navy’s newest carrier design, Lockheed Martin
Two aircraft conducted 34 flights, 122 catapult launches and 122 arrested landings during 11 days of testing aboard the pre-commissioning carrier John F. Kennedy.

image.alt: The F-35C Lightning II completed its first launch and recovery aboard a Gerald R. Ford-class aircraft carrier.

children: The significance extends beyond demonstrating that the aircraft can use a new flight deck. Compatibility between the F-35C and Ford-class carriers is a necessary step toward deploying the fighter’s stealth, sensors and data-sharing capabilities from the ships intended to support future carrier operations.
For defense investors, the tests mark progress in integrating two major military programs, although the announcement included no new contracts or changes to procurement plans.

The first recovery took place Oct. 13. The aircraft, based at Naval Air Station Patuxent River, Maryland, used Kennedy’s electromagnetic aircraft launch system and advanced arresting gear. Those systems, together with a redesigned flight deck and island, introduce different launch, landing and airflow conditions that require aircraft-specific testing.

The shipboard campaign followed shore-based trials conducted between January 2024 and May 2025. Test teams gathered data to verify launch-and-recovery software and installations, validate aircraft structural models and develop the operating bulletins that establish launch and recovery parameters. The work also assessed how the aircraft could be supported aboard the new carrier.

Testing included an initial use of Block 4 mission-systems software in a carrier environment, with teams collecting data to confirm software stability. That work broadens the campaign’s relevance beyond the mechanics of takeoff and landing to the integration of aircraft software and shipboard operations; it does not, by itself, establish that the full Block 4 upgrade is operationally ready.

F-35 development vice president, Sean Jackson, said completion of the test phase cleared the F-35C for operations across the Navy’s carrier fleet. The company also described the campaign as a step toward full operational integration aboard Ford-class ships, distinguishing the compatibility milestone from the broader work needed to prepare aircraft, crews and carriers for deployments.

title: F-35C tests advance integration with Navy’s new carrier class
